Here are practical things to look for and try when you go to the music store (based on what we discussed earlier about Les Pauls, open D tuning, and guitar features):

- Try the guitar in the tunings and styles you plan to play. If you use open D (D A D F# A D) or heavier fingerpicking, tune the guitar there and see how it feels and rings.
- Check string gauge and playability. Heavier strings (e.g. .012–.052 or .013–.056) suit lower tunings like open D and give fuller tone—ask if the store will fit a heavier set so you can test it.
- Evaluate pickups/tonal options. Les Paul–style humbuckers give warm, thick tone (great for rock) but can be heavy for delicate acoustic-like fingerpicking; guitars with coil-tap/coil-splitting give more tonal flexibility (single-coil–like brightness when tapped).
- Compare necks and feel. Body/neck construction affects comfort and tone: Stratocaster-style bolt-on, contoured bodies feel different from a Les Paul’s set neck and carved top—play both to see which neck profile and balance suit you.
- Check setup and action. Low action helps ease playing but make sure it’s set up so strings don’t buzz in your preferred tuning; ask the shop to demonstrate or adjust action if needed.
- Test sustain and resonance. Play chords and single-note lines to judge sustain (Les Pauls are known for strong sustain) and how the guitar responds to dynamics.
- Try fingerpicking and strumming. If you want to play acoustic-like fingerpicked parts, test how clear and articulated the guitar sounds when playing those patterns.
- Ask about electronics and switching options. If you value versatility, try guitars with pickup blends, coil-splits, or tone-shaping switches and listen for differences.
- Play through an amp and adjust amp settings. Tone is the combo of guitar and amp—try the guitar through an amp similar to what you’ll use and tweak EQ to hear its true character.
- Check build quality and comfort factors: fretwork, finish, weight, strap-button placement, and hardware reliability.
- Consider future needs: resale value, brand, and whether the guitar can be easily modified (pickups, tuners) if you want more options later.

If you have specific models in mind (e.g., Strat vs Les Paul), try both back-to-back and compare how each supports the genres and tunings you play. Happy shopping—and enjoy trying them out this weekend!
